title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
purpose: It sets out the duties of affection owed to fellow believers, parents (bodily and spiritual), kin, and neighbors, organizing each under the schema of obligatory rights and twelve manners.

points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred manners, forbids despising weak believers (saying God belittles and detests whoever despises a believer, and will not bring the two together on the Day of Resurrection unless he repents), forbids making a brother ask when his need is already known, and commands mutual visiting, tenderness, and giving, warning against being like the hypocrite who describes what he does not do.

Ali teaches that the Muslim is the mirror of his Muslim brother: on seeing a brother's slip one must not band together against him but guide, counsel, and treat him gently, and must avoid discord, which leads a person away from the path.

Ali forbids backbiting, citing the Qur'anic rebuke about eating the flesh of one's dead brother, and commands that believers meeting one another shake hands and show a bright face, so that by parting their burdens have lifted.

In a reported question-and-answer, Shaykh Shimon bin Muhammad al-Ghuri al-Hindi asked whether the Indian custom of asking neighbors for water, salt, or food (when one could afford to buy but lacks them at the moment) is permitted, and Sayyidina Hassan bin Idris (Badr al-Din) answered that there is no harm in it, since it belongs to the purity of affection and the excellence of brotherhood.

The Mustansiriya councils (seventeenth) place righteousness toward parents as the first of the twelve practices corresponding to the letters of the testimony, after the seven obligatory rights corresponding to its seven clauses.

The author notes that in both Qur'anic verses enjoining goodness toward parents, God commands goodness to both yet credits the child's account with the mother's deed alone (carrying him in hardship, in weakness upon weakness), so the one God distinguishes by mention must be distinguished with honor and righteousness.

Righteousness toward parents (eighteenth council) has seven obligatory parts and twelve manners, and extends to four levels: the bodily parents who caused his physical form, the two parents in religion who cause his form in knowledge (the Imam of the age and his proof), the two fathers of the community (the Prophet and the legatee, per the report 'I and you, O Ali, are the two fathers of this community,' and the Imams from their progeny), and finally righteousness toward one's own soul.

Righteousness toward one's own soul, the seal of this righteousness, consists in making the truth plain to the soul and establishing it there, magnifying it so as to awaken longing, placing fear in it, dealing gently with it, delivering it from what would destroy it, and rescuing it from what has bound it.

The twelve manners toward parents include honoring their dwelling, rising for them, answering their call, lowering the voice, not rebuking them, lowering the wing of humility, not walking ahead of them in light or darkness, never opposing their command or saying a word of complaint, desiring life for them in old age as they desired it for him in childhood, and providing for their needs as they provided for his.

The twenty-fourth council names three obligatory rights God will not accept unless discharged in full: the right of God (to leave what He forbade and enter what He commanded), the right of parents (thankfulness for what has passed and obedience in what remains), and the right of the child (to be raised with tenderness, nourished, and taught the Book and wisdom); Ali adds that whoever goes against his parents has been undutiful to them.

The nineteenth council divides a person's relatives into twelve categories (children; full brothers al-ashqa'; half-brothers by another mother banu al-'allat; half-brothers by the mother al-akhyaf; paternal grandfathers and grandmothers; maternal grandfathers and grandmothers; paternal uncles and aunts; maternal uncles and aunts), with anyone related through one of these taking that one's ruling, and requires keeping the tie, giving, drawing near, and loving even when the relatives cut off, withhold, push away, and abandon — and Ali adds that no oath binds in the severing of kinship.

The twentieth council divides safeguarding the neighbor (per the verse on the neighbor who is kin, the neighbor who is a stranger, and the companion at your side) into seven ranks — the believing kin-neighbor with three rights (neighborliness, kinship, faith); the kin-neighbor without faith with two; the believing stranger-neighbor with neighborliness and faith; the companion at your side who differs in religion with the right of neighborliness; the companion aboard the ship with the right of nearness; the sharer of one's litter; and the one who sits with you to receive wisdom, whose sanctity is the most binding and whose claim is most obligatory.

Twelve manners of neighborliness are enumerated — not peering into the neighbor's house, not listening in on his speech, not disclosing what one learns of him, not letting him hear or see what he would hate, not withholding a household implement when asked, not acting haughtily when of higher station, not envying him when he is above, helping when he seeks help, covering his 'awrah if exposed, causing him no injury, and bearing his injury with patience — these being the deeds of a people whose hearts God has tested for piety.
